prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: After the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The first round strengthened the case in the way I care about as an instrument builder. Four members now prefer it, five more name it as an alternative or say they would not block it, and nobody has raised a scientific objection to it. The physics is concrete and checked. The magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once. Fractional uncertainty has gone from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18, and independent clocks in several countries have been intercompared and agree. Those are the results I trust: calibration, systematics and independent confirmation. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the list, with the proposer and first demonstrator of the lattice scheme on one side and the group that took it to the accuracy and many-body frontier on the other. The citation I would defend ties the prize to the invention and its demonstrated accuracy. It deliberately does not rest on the redefinition of the second, which has not happened and is an argument for timeliness rather than merit. I answer the chair's question on what is new relative to 2005 and 2012 as follows. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and the ion-control prize recognised single quantum systems as clocks. The lattice clock adds a different regime, a large ensemble of neutral atoms held without shifting the transition, where statistics and systematics improve together. I regard that as a distinct contribution, though I ask the atomic-physics members to confirm it.
statement.case_against: The main risk is still overlap with the 1997, 2005 and 2012 prizes, and a sceptical reader can call the lattice clock a spectacular refinement of recognised ideas rather than a discovery about nature. No new physics has yet been seen with these clocks, and the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and constant-variation tests are partly prospective. Credit is also compressed into two names: Lemonde and the Paris group, other JILA and NIST contributors, and the ion-clock community have real claims, and the citation must not imply otherwise. Nobody on the committee, including me, has checked the magic-wavelength priority history from primary papers, and I am an astroparticle physicist who cannot settle the atomic-physics merit question alone. If an expert review found that the priority history does not separate cleanly, I would reconsider the credit.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B042 for robustness, citing the Z2 invariant as a band-topology result confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and by ARPES, and asks whether the credit omitting Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work is acceptable.
responses.response: I take your robustness argument seriously, and I agree B042 is mature and stable. This is why I keep it as my first alternative. Where I differ is on credit. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what pointed Molenkamp to HgTe, and Zhang's death means the prize cannot recognise it. The 3D experiments sit outside the three names. Any citation we write for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp must be narrow, limited to the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation, and you have said yourself that this is the weak point. I am also not the right person to say whether Z2 insulators are far enough from the 2016 prize, so I defer to you and Mehlig on that. My view is that the B037 credit has fewer open gaps today.

responses.point: Olsson argues that Kane and Mele together plus Molenkamp is the most defensible mapping of who did what first, that Mele must be included, and that the 2016 prize rewarded phase-transition topology rather than time-reversal-invariant band topology.
responses.response: Your distinction between the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz lineage and Z2 insulators is useful, and it answers the chair's question better than the rest of us could. A prediction followed by a measurement that nature could have refused is the structure I find most convincing in any experimental prize. I accept that dropping Mele would leave a gap in the theory credit, so B042 is better than B012 as the vehicle. My remaining concern is that your own list of omissions is long: Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and Xue. Because the cap is three people, I think B042 loses more credit than B037 does. I would be content to see B042 go forward if the committee prefers it, but I would write the citation as narrowly as you propose.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B037 with a citation tied to magic-wavelength trapping, says a third name is not supported, and states he would need a convincing answer on BHZ before ranking B042 above B037.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and on keeping to two names. I have no candidate for a third, and padding would weaken the text. On your disclosure about Boulder, I think it is fine to have it on record. You carry no tie to Ye or Katori, and your concern about Wallenberg Centre overlap applies to circuit QED, which is not in my configuration. I would add one point to your 'no new physics yet' caveat. For a measurement prize the figure of merit is the demonstrated uncertainty and its reproduction by other laboratories, and both are in place. We should still ask you and Lindroth to put the priority check in writing before the final ballot.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B006 as his preferred prize, calls the three leadership names a compromise, and says B037 is the better choice if the committee cannot defend that credit.
responses.response: Thank you for saying so openly. I agree the Higgs discovery is the best-confirmed result in the room, and I do not dispute that the experimental half has never been recognised. The question you ask me, as a particle physicist, is who the decisive contributors were at the time of discovery. I cannot name three people honestly. The discovery rests on the trigger, tracker and calorimeter teams, the analysis groups and the machine, and as you note the spokespersons at the time of discovery were different from the three founding names. I do not think I can defend those names under the statute. So I would take your fallback: if the committee concludes that B006 has no defensible attribution, B037 is the right place to land, and I would be glad to have your support for it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B037 first, warns that the credit is not perfectly clean (Lemonde, Le Targat, Boulder and NIST, ion clocks) and that her priority history is from memory, and opposes widening the citation to optical clocks in general.
responses.response: I agree that we should not widen the citation to optical clocks in general. Doing so would bring in the ion-clock programme and blur the 2012 overlap we are trying to avoid. A narrow wording about the magic-wavelength lattice keeps the claim that the committee can verify. I would ask you to be the one who states the priority question in a form an outside reviewer can check: what Katori proposed and first demonstrated, and what Ye's group added in accuracy, many-body behaviour and comb linkage. You have said you are recalling this from memory, and so are Kroll and Mehlig. I think that is the one evidence gap that could change my position, so an expert report is worth requesting.

uncertainties: The priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, relative to Ye's accuracy work and the Paris and Boulder groups, has not been checked from primary papers by anyone here. An expert report should confirm it before a final ballot.
Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes leave enough room for a lattice-clock prize is a judgement for the atomic-physics members. I rely on Lindroth, Johansson and Kroll for it.
Whether the exclusion of Lemonde, the Paris group and the ion-clock community can be explained in the citation without the prize seeming to dismiss them.

Whether B042 is a better prize than B037 depends on whether the committee can accept a narrow Kane, Mele and Molenkamp credit that leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work. I have not resolved this and I would follow the committee if it chose B042.

My own opening first choice, B003, has uncertain attribution among BeppoSAX, optical and radio follow-up teams, including a deceased contributor, and I no longer press it. It remains an alternative only.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my earlier disclosure. For B037 I have no personal, institutional or financial tie to Katori, Ye or their groups, and atomic clocks are outside my expertise. For B003 (gamma-ray burst afterglows) I have a general field affinity as a high-energy astrophysics instrument builder, and my work involves Fermi-LAT, but I have no tie to the credited names, and B003 is only an alternative. For B006 I have a CERN PhD background but no tie to ATLAS or CMS. As Chair I run the process and do not count hidden votes.
